claim: In moth flies (Clogmia, Lutzomyia), a maternal transcript isoform of odd-paired (Zic) is localized in the anterior egg and adopted the role of anterior determinant without essential protein change.
source: In moth flies (Clogmia, Lutzomyia), a maternal transcript isoform of odd-paired (Zic) is localized in the anterior egg and adopted the role of anterior determinant without essential protein change.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including RNA-seq, in situ hybridization, and functional RNAi experiments showing localization and function of odd-paired maternal transcript.

claim: Clogmia lost maternal germ plasm, which contributes to embryo polarity in fruit flies (Drosophila).
source: Additionally, Clogmia lost maternal germ plasm, which contributes to embryo polarity in fruit flies (Drosophila).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing absence of posteriorly localized maternal transcripts and absence of oskar homolog in Clogmia, along with zygotic expression of germ cell markers.

claim: In culicine (Culex, Aedes) mosquitoes, embryo polarity rests on a previously unnamed zinc finger gene (cucoid).
source: In culicine (Culex, Aedes) and anopheline mosquitoes (Anopheles), embryo polarity rests on a previously unnamed zinc finger gene (cucoid), or pangolin (dTcf), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis, RNA in situ hybridization, and RNAi experiments showing cucoid function in axis specification in Culex and Aedes.

claim: In anopheline mosquitoes (Anopheles), embryo polarity rests on pangolin (dTcf).
source: In culicine (Culex, Aedes) and anopheline mosquitoes (Anopheles), embryo polarity rests on a previously unnamed zinc finger gene (cucoid), or pangolin (dTcf), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis, RNA in situ hybridization, and RNAi experiments showing pangolin function in axis specification in Anopheles.

claim: Cucoid and pangolin localize an alternative transcript isoform at the anterior egg pole.
source: These genes also localize an alternative transcript isoform at the anterior egg pole.
evidence: This claim is supported by RACE experiments and RNA-seq data showing alternative transcript isoforms with distinct 3' ends that are localized at the anterior pole.

claim: Basal-branching crane flies (Nephrotoma) enrich maternal pangolin transcript at the anterior egg pole.
source: Basal-branching crane flies (Nephrotoma) also enrich maternal pangolin transcript at the anterior egg pole, suggesting that pangolin functioned as ancestral axis determinant in flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis and RNA in situ hybridization showing anterior localization of pangolin transcript in Nephrotoma.

claim: Pangolin functioned as ancestral axis determinant in flies.
source: Basal-branching crane flies (Nephrotoma) also enrich maternal pangolin transcript at the anterior egg pole, suggesting that pangolin functioned as ancestral axis determinant in flies.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that pangolin is localized in basal-branching crane flies and anopheline mosquitoes, suggesting an ancestral function.

claim: Alternative transcript isoforms with distinct expression can adopt fundamentally distinct developmental roles.
source: In conclusion, flies evolved an unexpected diversity of anterior determinants, and alternative transcript isoforms with distinct expression can adopt fundamentally distinct developmental roles.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that maternal and zygotic isoforms of odd-paired, cucoid, and pangolin have distinct expression patterns and functions in axis specification versus segmentation.

claim: Bicoid originated in the lineage of cyclorrhaphan flies more than 140 million years ago by duplication of zerknüllt (zen; aka Hox3).
source: The bicoid gene originated in the lineage of cyclorrhaphan flies more than 140 million years ago by duplication of zerknüllt (zen; aka Hox3), which, in insects, plays an important role in extraembryonic tissue development (Schmidt-Ott et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Schmidt-Ott et al., 2010.

claim: Zerknüllt plays an important role in extraembryonic tissue development in insects.
source: The bicoid gene originated in the lineage of cyclorrhaphan flies more than 140 million years ago by duplication of zerknüllt (zen; aka Hox3), which, in insects, plays an important role in extraembryonic tissue development (Schmidt-Ott et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Schmidt-Ott et al., 2010.

claim: Bicoid has not been found outside the cyclorrhaphan group.
source: The expression and function of cyclorrhaphan bicoid orthologs are conserved but bicoid has not been found outside this group, and has been lost in some lineages within the Cyclorrhapha.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies of bicoid distribution across fly lineages.

claim: Bicoid has been lost in some lineages within the Cyclorrhapha.
source: The expression and function of cyclorrhaphan bicoid orthologs are conserved but bicoid has not been found outside this group, and has been lost in some lineages within the Cyclorrhapha.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies of bicoid distribution across fly lineages.

claim: Panish evolved by gene duplication of the Tcf homolog pangolin (pan) and capture of the maternal promoter of a nucleoside kinase gene.
source: This gene evolved by gene duplication of the Tcf homolog pangolin (pan) and capture of the maternal promoter of a nucleoside kinase gene, and has been called panish (for pan"ish') (Klomp et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Klomp et al., 2015.

claim: Panish lacks the ß-catenin domain of Pangolin.
source: Pangolin functions as the effector of ß-catenin-dependent Wnt signaling pathway ('canonical' Wnt signaling) but Panish lacks the ß-catenin domain of Pangolin, and sequence similarity between Pangolin and Panish is limited to the cysteine-clamp domain (30 amino acids).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Klomp et al., 2015 and protein sequence analysis.

claim: Sequence similarity between Pangolin and Panish is limited to the cysteine-clamp domain (30 amino acids).
source: Pangolin functions as the effector of ß-catenin-dependent Wnt signaling pathway ('canonical' Wnt signaling) but Panish lacks the ß-catenin domain of Pangolin, and sequence similarity between Pangolin and Panish is limited to the cysteine-clamp domain (30 amino acids).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein sequence alignment data.

claim: Panish has not been found outside the family Chironomidae.
source: panish has not been found outside the family Chironomidae, suggesting that lower dipterans use different anterior determinants.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic analysis and genome searches in related species.

claim: The Clogmia genome contains a single odd-paired locus (Cal-opa).
source: The Clogmia genome contains a single odd-paired locus (Cal-opa) (Vicoso and Bachtrog, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to genome analysis by Vicoso and Bachtrog, 2015.

claim: Cal-opaMat encodes a truncated protein variant (635 amino acids), lacking the N-terminal 20 amino acids of Cal-OpaZyg.
source: Protein alignments with homologs from other flies suggest that Cal-opaZyg encodes the full-length Cal-Opa protein (655 amino acids), while Cal-opaMat encodes a truncated protein variant (635 amino acids), lacking the N-terminal 20 amino acids of Cal-OpaZyg (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cal-opaZyg encodes the full-length Cal-Opa protein (655 amino acids).
source: Protein alignments with homologs from other flies suggest that Cal-opaZyg encodes the full-length Cal-Opa protein (655 amino acids), while Cal-opaMat encodes a truncated protein variant (635 amino acids), lacking the N-terminal 20 amino acids of Cal-OpaZyg (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Cal-opaMat transcript was anteriorly localized in preblastoderm embryos but absent at the cellular blastoderm stage.
source: The Cal-opaMat transcript was anteriorly localized in preblastoderm embryos but absent at the cellular blastoderm stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Cal-opaZyg transcript was absent in preblastoderm embryos but expressed broadly in the trunk region of 7 hr-old blastoderm embryos.
source: Conversely, the Cal-opaZyg transcript was absent in preblastoderm embryos but expressed broadly in the trunk region of 7 hr-old blastoderm embryos (Figure 1D), like odd-paired in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Injection of Cal-opaMat double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) led to mirror-image duplications of the tail end (double abdomen).
source: Injection of Cal-opaMat double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) led to mirror-image duplications of the tail end (double abdomen; Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injection of dsRNA targeting Cal-opaZyg resulted in half the number of segmental expression domains of Cal-slp and caused defects in segmentation, dorsal closure, and head development but did not alter embryo polarity.
source: In contrast, injection of dsRNA targeting Cal-opaZyg resulted in half the number of segmental expression domains of Cal-slp (the ortholog of pair-rule gene sloppy-paired) and caused defects in segmentation, dorsal closure, and head development but did not alter embryo polarity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Injection of dsRNA targeting both Cal-opaMat and Cal-opaZyg resulted in double abdomens with missing segments.
source: Finally, injection of dsRNA targeting both Cal-opaMat and Cal-opaZyg resulted in double abdomens with missing segments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cal-opaMat and Cal-opaZyg have distinct roles in specifying embryo polarity and in segmentation, respectively.
source: These observations indicate distinct roles of Cal-opaMat and Cal-opaZyg in specifying embryo polarity and in segmentation, respectively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the distinct RNAi phenotypes of Cal-opaMat (double abdomen) and Cal-opaZyg (segmentation defects).

claim: Embryos injected with Cal-opaMat mRNA at the posterior pole expressed a head marker, Cal-otd, on both ends of the embryo and developed a symmetrical double head.
source: These embryos expressed a head marker, Cal-otd (ortholog of ocelliless/orthodenticle), on both ends of the embryo and developed a symmetrical double head, including some duplicated thoracic elements (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA injection experiments and marker gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Anterior enrichment of maternal transcripts other than Cal-opaMat mRNA is not essential for head development.
source: These observations suggest that anterior enrichment of maternal transcripts other than Cal-opaMat mRNA is not essential for head development, and that Cal-opaMat localization is sufficient for establishing embryo polarity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that posterior injection of Cal-opaMat alone is sufficient to induce ectopic head development.

claim: Cal-opaMat localization is sufficient for establishing embryo polarity.
source: These observations suggest that anterior enrichment of maternal transcripts other than Cal-opaMat mRNA is not essential for head development, and that Cal-opaMat localization is sufficient for establishing embryo polarity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that posterior injection of Cal-opaMat alone is sufficient to induce ectopic head development.

claim: Posterior injection of Cal-opaMat mRNA during the syncytial blastoderm stage (4 hr) resulted in embryos that developed with normal head-to-tail polarity.
source: To test this hypothesis, we conducted posterior injections of Cal-opaMat mRNA during the syncytial blastoderm stage (4 hr) and examined Cal-otd expression after gastrulation. These embryos developed with normal head-to-tail polarity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA injection experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Early timing of odd-paired activity is essential for its function as anterior determinant.
source: This result places the requirement of odd-paired for axis specification prior to the syncytial blastoderm stage and suggests that early timing of odd-paired activity is essential for its function as anterior determinant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that late injection of Cal-opaMat does not induce double heads.

claim: Posterior injection of Cal-opaZyg mRNA at the posterior pole of preblastoderm embryos resulted in embryos that developed as double heads.
source: To test whether the open reading frame difference is required for the anterior determinant function, we injected Cal-opaZyg mRNA at the posterior pole of preblastoderm embryos. Embryos from this experiment also developed as double heads (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA injection experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Posterior injection of Cal-opaZyg-Met21Leu mRNA resulted in double heads.
source: Because the translation start site of Cal-OpaMat is located downstream of the Cal-OpaZyg translation start site, we also tested Cal-opaZyg mRNA in which the putative start codon for Cal-OpaMat was mutated to encode leucine (Cal-opaZyg-Met21Leu). Posterior injection of Cal-opaZyg-Met21Leu mRNA also resulted in double heads (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA injection experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The protein difference between Cal-OpaMat and Cal-OpaZyg is not essential for the anterior determinant function of odd-paired in Clogmia.
source: These findings indicate that the protein difference between Cal-OpaMat and Cal-OpaZyg is not essential for the anterior determinant function of odd-paired in Clogmia.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both Cal-opaZyg and Cal-opaZyg-Met21Leu can induce double heads when injected posteriorly.

claim: mRNAs of protein variants with large N-terminal truncation (Cal-Opa115-655 and Cal-Opa182-655) retained the ability to induce double heads.
source: mRNAs of protein variants with large N-terminal truncation (Cal-Opa115-655 and Cal-Opa182-655) retained the ability to induce double heads.
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA injection experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: mRNAs of protein variants with C-terminal truncation (Cal-Opa182-445 and Cal-Opa1-337+22) failed to induce double heads.
source: However, mRNAs of protein variants with C-terminal truncation (Cal-Opa182-445 and Cal-Opa1-337+22, a hypothetical splice variant) failed to induce double heads.
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA injection experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ability of Cal-Opa to specify embryo polarity requires the C-terminal portion of the protein but is largely insensitive to N-terminal truncation.
source: These results indicate that the ability of Cal-Opa to specify embryo polarity requires the C-terminal portion of the protein but is largely insensitive to N-terminal truncation, corroborating our above conclusion that N-terminal differences between Cal-OpaMat and Cal-OpaZyg were not essential for evolving the anterior determinant function of Cal-opa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the truncation experiments showing that N-terminal truncations retain function while C-terminal truncations do not.

claim: Expression profiling of anterior and posterior egg halves in Clogmia did not reveal any posteriorly localized maternal transcripts.
source: However, in Clogmia, expression profiling of anterior and posterior egg halves did not reveal any posteriorly localized maternal transcripts (Figure 1B, alpha = 0.001, unadj.), and no oskar homolog was found in our Clogmia transcriptomes or the Clogmia genome (Vicoso and Bachtrog, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1B and genome searches.

claim: No oskar homolog was found in Clogmia transcriptomes or the Clogmia genome.
source: However, in Clogmia, expression profiling of anterior and posterior egg halves did not reveal any posteriorly localized maternal transcripts (Figure 1B, alpha = 0.001, unadj.), and no oskar homolog was found in our Clogmia transcriptomes or the Clogmia genome (Vicoso and Bachtrog, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome and genome searches.

claim: Cal-nos1, Cal-nos3, and Cal-nos4 were not localized in the posterior of preblastoderm embryos but were expressed in a small set of cells at the posterior pole of cellular blastoderm and gastrulating embryos.
source: Cal-nos1, Cal-nos3, and Cal-nos4 were not localized in the posterior of preblastoderm embryos but were expressed in a small set of cells at the posterior pole of cellular blastoderm and gastrulating embryos along with Cal-vas, Cal-tud, and Cal-gcl that were expressed more broadly (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Clogmia lacks maternal germ plasm.
source: These observations suggest that Clogmia lacks maternal germ plasm and that Clogmia may induce the germ cell fate zygotically.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of posteriorly localized maternal transcripts and the zygotic expression pattern of germ cell markers.

claim: Clogmia may induce the germ cell fate zygotically.
source: These observations suggest that Clogmia lacks maternal germ plasm and that Clogmia may induce the germ cell fate zygotically.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the zygotic expression pattern of germ cell markers and the duplication of Cal-nos positive cells in double abdomens.

claim: Cal-nos positive cells were duplicated in double abdomens.
source: To test this hypothesis, we examined Cal-nos expression in Cal-opaMat RNAi embryos. Cal-nos positive cells were duplicated in double abdomens (Figure 2E), indicating that Clogmia uses an inductive mechanism for germ cell specification, which is repressed in the anterior embryo by Cal-opaMat.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data in RNAi embryos shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Clogmia uses an inductive mechanism for germ cell specification, which is repressed in the anterior embryo by Cal-opaMat.
source: Cal-nos positive cells were duplicated in double abdomens (Figure 2E), indicating that Clogmia uses an inductive mechanism for germ cell specification, which is repressed in the anterior embryo by Cal-opaMat.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the duplication of germ cells in double abdomens, suggesting that germ cell fate is induced in the absence of anterior determinant.

claim: Axis specification in the Clogmia embryo is independent from germ cell specification.
source: Therefore, axis specification in the Clogmia embryo is independent from germ cell specification.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Clogmia lacks maternal germ plasm and uses zygotic induction for germ cell specification.

claim: Clogmia is the first example of inductive germ cell specification in flies.
source: To our knowledge, Clogmia is also the first example of inductive germ cell specification in flies.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of germ cell specification mechanisms in other fly species and the novel finding in Clogmia.

claim: Maternal odd-paired transcript is absent in freshly deposited eggs of chironomids and mosquitoes.
source: Maternal odd-paired transcript is absent in freshly deposited eggs of chironomids (Klomp et al., 2015) and mosquitoes (Akbari et al., 2013), both of which belong to the Culicomorpha lineage (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Klomp et al., 2015 and Akbari et al., 2013.

claim: The most enriched maternal transcript in the anterior half of 1–2 hr old Lutzomyia embryos was homologous to odd-paired.
source: Of 5392 annotated transcripts, the most enriched maternal transcript in the anterior half of 1–2 hr old embryos was homologous to odd-paired and was therefore named Llo-opaMat (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The most enriched transcript in the posterior Lutzomyia embryo was homologous to oskar.
source: In the posterior Lutzomyia embryo, the most enriched transcript was homologous to oskar, indicating that Lutzomyia eggs contain maternal germ plasm at the posterior pole, unlike the Clogmia eggs.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lutzomyia eggs contain maternal germ plasm at the posterior pole, unlike the Clogmia eggs.
source: In the posterior Lutzomyia embryo, the most enriched transcript was homologous to oskar, indicating that Lutzomyia eggs contain maternal germ plasm at the posterior pole, unlike the Clogmia eggs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of posteriorly localized oskar transcript in Lutzomyia.

claim: A broad range of moth flies use odd-paired transcript as anterior determinant.
source: These findings suggest that a broad range of moth flies use odd-paired transcript as anterior determinant, and that maternal germ plasm was lost only in the Clogmia lineage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both Clogmia and Lutzomyia use odd-paired as anterior determinant.

claim: Maternal germ plasm was lost only in the Clogmia lineage.
source: These findings suggest that a broad range of moth flies use odd-paired transcript as anterior determinant, and that maternal germ plasm was lost only in the Clogmia lineage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of oskar in Lutzomyia but not in Clogmia.

claim: Llo-opaMat and Llo-opaZyg share the same open reading frame but differ at their untranslated 5' and 3' ends.
source: Llo-opaMat and Llo-opaZyg share the same open reading frame but differ at their untranslated 5' and 3' ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by RACE experiments and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-terminal ends of Llo-OpaMat/Llo-OpaZyg and Cal-OpaZyg proteins are homologous.
source: Since the N-terminal ends of Llo-OpaMat/Llo-OpaZyg and Cal-OpaZyg proteins are homologous (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we infer that the N-terminal truncation of Cal-OpaMat occurred after the transcript had evolved maternal expression and anterior localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal truncation of Cal-OpaMat occurred after the transcript had evolved maternal expression and anterior localization.
source: Since the N-terminal ends of Llo-OpaMat/Llo-OpaZyg and Cal-OpaZyg proteins are homologous (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we infer that the N-terminal truncation of Cal-OpaMat occurred after the transcript had evolved maternal expression and anterior localization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of protein sequences between Clogmia and Lutzomyia.

claim: Odd-paired homologs from Lutzomyia, Chironomus, and Drosophila induced double heads in Clogmia when injected with the endogenous kozak sequence of Cal-opaMat.
source: To test this possibility, we injected odd-paired mRNA from Lutzomyia, Chironomus, or Drosophila into the posterior pole of early Clogima embryos. All of these odd-paired homologs induced double heads in Clogmia, provided that the endogenous kozak sequence of Cal-opaMat was used for optimal translation efficiency (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA injection experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Amino acid substitutions were not essential for the evolution of the anterior determinant function of odd-paired in moth flies.
source: Since neither Drosophila nor Chironomus uses odd-paired for specifying embryo polarity, these results suggest that amino acid substitutions were not essential for the evolution of the anterior determinant function of odd-paired in moth flies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that odd-paired homologs from species that do not use it as anterior determinant can still function as such in Clogmia.

claim: The anterior determinant function of odd-paired in moth flies evolved via co-option when alternative maternal transcript of moth fly odd-paired became enriched at the anterior egg pole.
source: We therefore propose that this gene function evolved via co-option when alternative maternal transcript of moth fly odd-paired became enriched at the anterior egg pole.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that odd-paired homologs from other species can function as anterior determinant without specific amino acid changes.

claim: The most enriched transcript in the anterior embryo of Culex was closely related to an uncharacterized gene of Drosophila (CG9215).
source: The most enriched transcript in the anterior embryo was closely related to an uncharacterized gene of Drosophila (CG9215).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4A and BLAST searches.

claim: CG9215 belongs to a poorly defined larger gene family in Drosophila that might be represented by a single gene in mosquitoes.
source: However, reciprocal BLAST searches suggest that CG9215 belongs to a poorly defined larger gene family in Drosophila that might be represented by a single gene in mosquitoes.
evidence: This claim is based on reciprocal BLAST analysis.

claim: Cucoid encodes a protein with five C2H2 zinc finger domains.
source: cucoid encodes a protein with five C2H2 zinc finger domains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only cucoidB and cucoidC were recovered from cDNA of 0–2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos.
source: RACE experiments with cDNA from 0 to 7 hr-old embryos revealed three alternative cucoid transcripts with distinct 3' ends (cucoidA, cucoidB, and cucoidC) (Figure 4B), but only cucoidB and cucoidC were recovered from cDNA of 0–2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos, suggesting that one or both these transcripts might be maternally localized at the anterior pole.
evidence: This claim is supported by RACE experiments.

claim: Only the cucoidC isoform is maternally localized at the anterior pole.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that only the cucoidC isoform is maternally localized at the anterior pole and could function as anterior determinant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from RNA in situ hybridization data showing that only the probe against all three isoforms detected anterior localization in preblastoderm embryos.

claim: Many embryos injected with cucoid dsRNA expressed Cqu-cad in the anterior and underwent ectopic gastrulation at the anterior pole.
source: To test this hypothesis, we injected cucoid dsRNA from the shared 5' region and examined the expression of a posterior marker (Cqu-cad) in gastrulating embryos. Many of these embryos expressed Cqu-cad in the anterior and underwent ectopic gastrulation at the anterior pole, suggesting that normal head-to-tail polarity was lost (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments and marker gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cucoid acquired the anterior determinant function via the localization of a maternal transcript isoform with an alternative 3' end.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that cucoid acquired the anterior determinant function via the localization of a maternal transcript isoform with an alternative 3' end.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the identification of alternative 3' isoforms and the anterior localization of cucoidC.

claim: Expression profiling of Aedes embryos identified cucoid (Aae-cucoid) as the gene with the most significantly enriched transcript in the anterior embryo.
source: In this species, expression profiling of 5802 transcripts from the anterior and posterior transcriptomes of 1 hr-old preblastoderm embryos also identified cucoid (Aae-cucoid) as the gene with the most significantly enriched transcript in the anterior embryo (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RACE experiments with Aedes cDNA revealed three similar Aae-cucoid transcripts with alternative 3' ends.
source: RACE experiments with cDNA from 1 hr to 6 hr-old embryos revealed three similar Aae-cucoid transcripts with alternative 3' ends (Aae-cucoidA, Aae-cucoidB, and Aae-cucoidC) (Figure 5B), and RNA in situ hybridization experiments with a probe against all three isoforms confirmed the anterior localization of Aae-cucoid transcript in preblastoderm embryos (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RACE experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RNA in situ hybridization experiments confirmed the anterior localization of Aae-cucoid transcript in preblastoderm embryos.
source: RACE experiments with cDNA from 1 hr to 6 hr-old embryos revealed three similar Aae-cucoid transcripts with alternative 3' ends (Aae-cucoidA, Aae-cucoidB, and Aae-cucoidC) (Figure 5B), and RNA in situ hybridization experiments with a probe against all three isoforms confirmed the anterior localization of Aae-cucoid transcript in preblastoderm embryos (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Injection of Aae-cucoid dsRNA resulted in double abdomens.
source: Injection of Aae-cucoid dsRNA against the shared region of all transcripts resulted in double abdomens (Figure 5D), suggesting that cucoid evolved its function as anterior determinant prior to the divergence of the Culex and Aedes lineages.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cucoid evolved its function as anterior determinant prior to the divergence of the Culex and Aedes lineages.
source: Injection of Aae-cucoid dsRNA against the shared region of all transcripts resulted in double abdomens (Figure 5D), suggesting that cucoid evolved its function as anterior determinant prior to the divergence of the Culex and Aedes lineages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that cucoid functions as anterior determinant in both Culex and Aedes.

claim: Whole mount RNA in situ hybridizations with a probe against the Anopheles gambiae ortholog of cucoid did not detect any anterior localized transcript in 1 hr-old embryos.
source: Whole mount RNA in situ hybridizations with a probe against the Anopheles gambiae ortholog of cucoid did not detect any anterior localized transcript in 1 hr-old embryos, suggesting that Anopheles uses a different anterior determinant than Culex and Aedes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Anopheles uses a different anterior determinant than Culex and Aedes.
source: Whole mount RNA in situ hybridizations with a probe against the Anopheles gambiae ortholog of cucoid did not detect any anterior localized transcript in 1 hr-old embryos, suggesting that Anopheles uses a different anterior determinant than Culex and Aedes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of anterior localized cucoid transcript in Anopheles.

claim: The most enriched transcript in the anterior embryo of Anopheles gambiae was homologous to pangolin.
source: In the anterior embryo, the most enriched transcript was homologous to pangolin (also known as Tcf) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Two alternative transcript variants of pangolin in Anopheles were identified with non-overlapping 3'UTRs but nearly identical open reading frames.
source: To test for potential alternative maternal and zygotic isoforms of pangolin in Anopheles, we mapped the assembled transcripts and 5' and 3' RACE products from 1 to 6 hr-old embryos onto an available A. gambiae genome assembly (AgamP4). We identified two alternative transcript variants with non-overlapping 3'UTRs but nearly identical open reading frames that we named Aga-panMat and Aga-panZyg, respectively (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RACE experiments and RNA-seq mapping shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aga-panMat was tightly localized at the anterior pole of 1–2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos and only weakly expressed in elongated germbands.
source: Aga-panMat was tightly localized at the anterior pole of 1–2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos and only weakly expressed in elongated germbands, whereas Aga-panZyg was expressed segmentally in elongated germbands but not in embryos younger than 2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Aga-panZyg was expressed segmentally in elongated germbands but not in embryos younger than 2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos.
source: Aga-panMat was tightly localized at the anterior pole of 1–2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos and only weakly expressed in elongated germbands, whereas Aga-panZyg was expressed segmentally in elongated germbands but not in embryos younger than 2 hr-old preblastoderm embryos (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both pangolin isoforms were conserved in Anopheles coluzzii with sequence identity above 99%.
source: Both pangolin isoforms were conserved in Anopheles coluzzii with sequence identity above 99% and the maternal isoform (Aco-panMat) was localized at the anterior pole (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison and RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The stage-specific expression of both pangolin isoforms was conserved outside the Anopheles gambiae species complex in Anopheles stephensi.
source: The stage-specific expression of both pangolin isoforms was also conserved outside the Anopheles gambiae species complex in Anopheles stephensi (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In Anopheles, the maternal variant of pangolin includes an additional seven amino acids at C-terminal end due to alternative polyadenylation and splicing.
source: Alignments of dipteran Pangolin proteins suggest that, in Anopheles, the maternal variant includes an additional seven amino acids at C-terminal end due to alternative polyadenylation and splicing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injection of Aco-panMat-specific dsRNA into A. coluzzii embryos resulted in anterior truncations and, in extreme cases, double abdomens.
source: Injection of Aco-panMat-specific dsRNA into several hundred 1 hr-old A. coluzzii embryos resulted in only 37 cuticles with variable phenotypes, including anterior truncations and, in extreme cases, double abdomens (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Injection of Aco-panZyg-specific dsRNA into A. coluzzii embryos resulted in severe segmentation defects but no double abdomens or anterior-specific truncation defects.
source: Injection of Aco-panZyg-specific dsRNA into 1 hr-old A. coluzzii embryos resulted in severe segmentation defects that were difficult to characterize, but no double abdomens or anterior-specific truncation defects were found (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Pangolin acquired the anterior determinant function via the localization of a maternal transcript isoform with an alternative 3' end.
source: Taken together with the isoform-specific transcript localization data presented above, these RNAi results support the hypothesis that pangolin acquired the anterior determinant function via the localization of a maternal transcript isoform with an alternative 3' end.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the isoform-specific expression patterns and RNAi phenotypes.

claim: The most enriched transcript in the posterior embryo of Nephrotoma was related to oskar.
source: The most enriched transcript in the posterior embryo was related to oskar, suggesting that crane fly eggs contain maternal germ plasm at the posterior pole.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Crane fly eggs contain maternal germ plasm at the posterior pole.
source: The most enriched transcript in the posterior embryo was related to oskar, suggesting that crane fly eggs contain maternal germ plasm at the posterior pole.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of posteriorly localized oskar transcript.

claim: The most enriched transcript in the anterior embryo of Nephrotoma was homologous to pangolin.
source: The most enriched transcript in the anterior embryo was homologous to pangolin and therefore named Nsu-pan.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The anterior localization of Nsu-pan transcript was confirmed by RNA in situ hybridization.
source: The anterior localization of this transcript was confirmed by RNA in situ hybridization (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Ancestral dipteran insects localized maternal pangolin transcript in the anterior egg pole.
source: Taken together with our Anopheles data, our results in Nephrotoma suggest that ancestral dipteran insects localized maternal pangolin transcript in the anterior egg pole, where this transcript may have functioned as anterior determinant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both basal crane flies and anopheline mosquitoes localize pangolin transcript anteriorly.

claim: Maternal pangolin transcript may have functioned as anterior determinant in ancestral dipteran insects.
source: Taken together with our Anopheles data, our results in Nephrotoma suggest that ancestral dipteran insects localized maternal pangolin transcript in the anterior egg pole, where this transcript may have functioned as anterior determinant.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the inference from localization patterns in basal and derived dipteran lineages.

claim: Only panish mRNA rescued panish RNAi embryos.
source: Only panish mRNA rescued panish RNAi embryos (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B), suggesting that panish co-evolved with its targets and functionally diverged after its origin via gene duplication from pangolin.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Panish co-evolved with its targets and functionally diverged after its origin via gene duplication from pangolin.
source: Only panish mRNA rescued panish RNAi embryos (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B), suggesting that panish co-evolved with its targets and functionally diverged after its origin via gene duplication from pangolin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that pangolin cannot substitute for panish in rescue experiments.

claim: Alternative transcription facilitates the evolution of anterior determinants by providing the UTR sequence for isoform-specific localization signals that do not interfere with other gene functions.
source: Since anterior determinants are localized in the anterior egg, and signals for the subcellular localization of transcripts are typically found in UTRs (Holt and Bullock, 2009), it is possible that alternative transcription facilitates the evolution of anterior determinants by providing the UTR sequence for isoform-specific localization signals that do not interfere with other gene functions.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on known principles of RNA localization and the observation of alternative UTRs in anterior determinants.

claim: Signals for the subcellular localization of transcripts are typically found in UTRs.
source: Since anterior determinants are localized in the anterior egg, and signals for the subcellular localization of transcripts are typically found in UTRs (Holt and Bullock, 2009), it is possible that alternative transcription facilitates the evolution of anterior determinants by providing the UTR sequence for isoform-specific localization signals that do not interfere with other gene functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Holt and Bullock, 2009.

claim: Alternative last exons of transcript isoforms confer isoform-specific localization in neurons.
source: For example, it has been shown that alternative last exons of transcript isoforms confer isoform-specific localization in neurons (Taliaferro et al., 2016; Ciolli Mattioli et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taliaferro et al., 2016 and Ciolli Mattioli et al., 2019.

claim: Panish inherited its function from pangolin.
source: We therefore propose that panish, which evolved from pangolin via gene duplication in the Chironominae lineage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), inherited its function from pangolin.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that pangolin functions as anterior determinant in ancestral dipterans and panish evolved from pangolin.

claim: A maternal zerknüllt isoform may have become localized at the anterior pole of the egg and acquired the role of anterior determinant via co-option, prior to the origin of bicoid via gene duplication.
source: However, in analogy with our findings, it is also possible that a maternal zerknüllt isoform became localized at the anterior pole of the egg and acquired the role of anterior determinant via co-option, prior to the origin of bicoid via gene duplication (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an alternative hypothesis for the evolution of bicoid based on analogy with the findings for odd-paired, cucoid, and pangolin.

claim: The Q50K mutation in the homeodomain of Bicoid may have been a secondary, potentially maladaptive change.
source: If bicoid inherited its function from zerknüllt, the Q50K mutation in the homeodomain of Bicoid must have been a secondary, potentially maladaptive change.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the hypothesis that bicoid inherited its function from zerknüllt.

claim: The Q50K mutation may have been fixed in the cyclorrhaphan stem lineage via a compensatory or balancing mechanism and would have driven co-evolution of its targets.
source: In this case, it may have been fixed in the cyclorrhaphan stem lineage via a compensatory or balancing mechanism and would have driven co-evolution of its targets.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the fixation of the Q50K mutation.

claim: The evolutionary origin and divergence of panish and bicoid could have served the purpose of reducing the pleiotropy of their progenitor genes, pangolin and zerknüllt.
source: If panish and bicoid inherited their functions, their evolutionary origin and divergence could have served the purpose of reducing the pleiotropy of their progenitor genes, pangolin and zerknüllt, rather than allowing them to take on an entirely new function in development.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an evolutionary explanation for gene duplication and divergence.

claim: Alternative transcription is a widespread phenomenon.
source: Recent genome-wide analyses have shown that alternative transcription is a widespread phenomenon.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from recent genome-wide studies.

claim: There are on average four alternative transcription start sites per gene in humans.
source: For example, there are on average four alternative transcription start sites per gene in humans (Forrest et al., 2014) and at least 50–70% of mammalian genes are subject to alternative polyadenylation (Shepard et al., 2011; Adams et al., 2000; Derti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Forrest et al., 2014.

claim: At least 50–70% of mammalian genes are subject to alternative polyadenylation.
source: For example, there are on average four alternative transcription start sites per gene in humans (Forrest et al., 2014) and at least 50–70% of mammalian genes are subject to alternative polyadenylation (Shepard et al., 2011; Adams et al., 2000; Derti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shepard et al., 2011; Adams et al., 2000; Derti et al., 2012.

claim: Alternative transcript isoforms can be tightly regulated in a cell or tissue specific manner.
source: Alternative transcript isoforms can be tightly regulated in a cell or tissue specific manner and can affect transcription and translation efficiency as well as splicing (An et al., 2008; Davuluri et al., 2008; Lau et al., 2010; Pinto et al., 2011; Smibert et al., 2012; Anvar et al., 2018; Tushev et al., 2018; Taliaferro et al., 2016; Ciolli Mattioli et al., 2019; Shabalina et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Alternative transcription can generate dominant negative and alternatively localized protein isoforms.
source: Functional studies in model organisms have shown that alternative transcription can generate dominant negative and alternatively localized protein isoforms (Davuluri et al., 2008; Bharti et al., 2008; Vacik et al., 2011; Berkovits and Mayr, 2015; Schrankel et al., 2016), while misregulation of alternative transcript isoforms has been associated with human diseases including cancer (Mayr and Bartel, 2009; Wiesner et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012; Shapiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple functional studies.

claim: Misregulation of alternative transcript isoforms has been associated with human diseases including cancer.
source: Functional studies in model organisms have shown that alternative transcription can generate dominant negative and alternatively localized protein isoforms (Davuluri et al., 2008; Bharti et al., 2008; Vacik et al., 2011; Berkovits and Mayr, 2015; Schrankel et al., 2016), while misregulation of alternative transcript isoforms has been associated with human diseases including cancer (Mayr and Bartel, 2009; Wiesner et al., 2015; Pal et al., 2012; Shapiro et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies linking alternative transcript isoforms to disease.

claim: A large fraction of alternative promoter sequences is conserved between human and mice.
source: For example, a large fraction of alternative promoter sequences is conserved between human and mice, but those with cell or tissue restricted expression have frequently changed during mammalian evolution (Baek et al., 2007; Forrest et al., 2014), suggesting that alternative promoters may have played a significant role in cell type evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baek et al., 2007 and Forrest et al., 2014.

claim: Alternative promoters with cell or tissue restricted expression have frequently changed during mammalian evolution.
source: For example, a large fraction of alternative promoter sequences is conserved between human and mice, but those with cell or tissue restricted expression have frequently changed during mammalian evolution (Baek et al., 2007; Forrest et al., 2014), suggesting that alternative promoters may have played a significant role in cell type evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baek et al., 2007 and Forrest et al., 2014.

claim: Alternative promoters may have played a significant role in cell type evolution.
source: For example, a large fraction of alternative promoter sequences is conserved between human and mice, but those with cell or tissue restricted expression have frequently changed during mammalian evolution (Baek et al., 2007; Forrest et al., 2014), suggesting that alternative promoters may have played a significant role in cell type evolution.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that alternative promoters with tissue-specific expression have changed during evolution.

claim: Protein terminal ends generated by alternative transcription commonly contain intrinsically disordered regions which are enriched in sites that mediate protein-protein interactions.
source: Another likely substrate for evolutionary diversification are the protein terminal ends generated by alternative transcription in conjunction with alternative splicing. These terminal ends commonly contain intrinsically disordered regions which are enriched in sites that mediate protein-protein interactions (Buljan et al., 2013; Shabalina et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buljan et al., 2013 and Shabalina et al., 2014.

claim: A light fur color variant of beach mice evolved repeatedly via selection for an alternative agouti isoform with increased translation efficiency.
source: A recent case study found that a light fur color variant of beach mice evolved repeatedly via selection for an alternative agouti isoform with increased translation efficiency (Linnen et al., 2013; Mallarino et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Linnen et al., 2013 and Mallarino et al., 2017.

claim: Differential expression of alternative transcript isoforms can result in the evolution of new gene functions, independent of, and prior to gene duplication and sub-functionalization.
source: Therefore, we propose that differential expression of alternative transcript isoforms can result in the evolution of new gene functions, independent of, and prior to gene duplication and sub-functionalization.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the findings that three old genes evolved anterior determinant function via alternative transcript isoforms.

claim: Alternative transcription could play an important role in the evolution of gene regulatory networks.
source: Given that alternative transcription is a widespread phenomenon, it could play an important role in the evolution of gene regulatory networks.
evidence: This claim is speculative, extrapolating from the findings in this study to a broader evolutionary principle.
